author: reek
body: This chapter never compiled until 2026-07-20, so none of it had ever run: encrypt-payload called aesgcm-encrypt with three arguments where it takes four, decrypt-payload passed the tag where the AAD goes, and create-team-share threw the authentication tag away because TeamKeyShare had no field to hold one.

author: reek
body: A round-trip alone cannot see any of that -- two halves that share a mistake agree with each other perfectly. So the assertions that carry weight here are the ones that must FAIL to pass: a tampered ciphertext, a tampered tag, and a wrong derivation must each come back None. Before the tag field existed, the tampered-tag case could not even be written down.

author: reek
body: The key derivation is checked against hkdf called directly, which is the same primitive by a different route: it pins that derive-vault-key passes the salt and the info string it claims to, which is exactly what was wrong.

author: reek
body: list-set-at writes in place and hands back the same list, so a tampered copy has to be built first or the original is tampered too.

author: reek
body: derive-vault-key must hand hkdf the master salt and the vault-scoped info string. Computing the same thing here through hkdf directly is what makes a dropped salt visible; a round-trip would not notice, because encrypt and decrypt would both drop it.

author: reek
body: Two secrets in one vault must not share a key.

author: reek
body: The nonce is twelve bytes, not the eight words sha256 actually returns. This is the assertion that catches the words-for-bytes confusion the DevelopersGuide warns about.

author: reek
body: Negative controls. Each of these must come back None, and a compressor-style "agrees with itself" implementation cannot satisfy them.

author: reek
body: __record-set stores into the record and returns the same one, so a tampered variant needs its own EncryptedSecret rather than a mutation of the shared fixture.
